The column widths of a table that gives none

Source: R/default_widths.R
default_col_widths.Rd

The proportions rtftable() uses when a table gives no widths (no col_rel_width, column_widths_twips, or a plan's plan_columns(widths = )): the row-heading columns as wide as their longest line, within a share of the table (at most 40%; less with many data columns, down to 20%; 5 points more when the rows are indented), the data columns sharing the rest equally, and a data column whose longest cell does not fit widened from the others. A program that wants these as its starting point writes them out: col_rel_width = default_col_widths(data) gives the same table (to a few twips of rounding at the default digits = 1), and is then changed by hand.

Usage

default_col_widths(
  data,
  row_title = NULL,
  col_header = NULL,
  width_chars = 120,
  digits = 1L
)

Arguments

data

A data frame: the table's body, as it prints.

row_title

The row-heading columns, by position or name; NULL (default) is column 1, as in rtftable().

col_header

The column header's labels (one row, or a list of rows: only the last is counted), or NULL for names(data). A header wraps, so it counts by its longest word.

width_chars

The table's width in characters of its font: 120 (the default) is a landscape letter or A4 page in a 9-point monospace font. It decides whether a long cell fits its share.

digits

The proportions are rounded to this many decimals and scaled so the smallest data column is 1.

Value

A named numeric vector, one per column of data: relative widths, as col_rel_width (and plan_columns(widths = )) take them.

See also

auto_col_widths() (widths in twips from the content alone).

Examples

df <- data.frame(Characteristic = c("Age (years)", "  Mean (SD)", "  Median"),
                 Placebo = c("", "75.2 (8.59)", "76.0"),
                 Active  = c("", "74.4 (7.89)", "75.0"))
default_col_widths(df)
#> Characteristic        Placebo         Active 
#>            0.4            1.0            1.0
